paragraphs: This paper broadens the conditions under which adaptive proximal gradient methods can solve convex optimization problems. Traditional analyses often require Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, which limits how quickly gradients can change. The authors show that a class of methods can still converge under the weaker condition of local Hölder gradient continuity, including continuously differentiable semi-algebraic functions.

The central contribution is an analysis that handles this weaker regularity without introducing approximation or a linesearch. Existing approaches often use approximate information through epsilon-oracles or repeatedly test candidate steps through linesearch procedures. Here, plain Hölder inequalities supply the mathematical control needed to retain the original adaptive, linesearch-free approach.

The authors prove convergence of the full sequence of iterates without requiring advance knowledge of the local Hölder constants or continuity order. This matters because the method need not be supplied with those regularity parameters to obtain the stated guarantee. Experiments compare it with baseline methods on machine-learning tasks with both local and global Hölder continuity.
icml-2024-adaptive-proximal-gradient-met.tldr: Adaptive proximal gradient methods can converge for convex problems under local Hölder gradient continuity without approximation, linesearch, or prior knowledge of the continuity parameters.

paragraphs: Deep Stochastic Mechanics introduces a deep-learning approach to simulating the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The computational problem becomes difficult as the number of dimensions grows: the abstract describes existing approaches whose cost increases exponentially with dimension. The proposed method draws on stochastic mechanics and generative diffusion models to seek a more economical representation of the evolving wave function.

Its main mechanism is sampling from a Markovian diffusion that can adapt to low-dimensional structure hidden within the wave function. The potential saving therefore depends on the latent dimension, rather than following automatically from a large ambient dimension. When that underlying structure is sufficiently compact, the method may have substantially lower computational cost in high-dimensional problems.

The paper also proposes new equations for stochastic quantum mechanics with quadratic computational complexity in the number of dimensions. Numerical simulations support the theoretical findings and show a significant advantage over other deep-learning approaches considered for quantum mechanics. Together, these contributions connect a structure-adaptive sampling method with a more computationally manageable mathematical formulation.
icml-2024-deep-stochastic-mechanics-6b95.tldr: Deep Stochastic Mechanics uses diffusion sampling and new stochastic quantum equations to reduce the computational burden of simulating evolving wave functions.

paragraphs: Mapper represents a dataset as a graph whose connected components, branches, and loops correspond to topological structures in the data. This makes it useful for unsupervised representation and visualization, but its output depends on several manually selected parameters. A particularly consequential choice is the filter, a continuous function whose variation across the data guides construction of the graph.

The paper addresses how to optimize that filter. Earlier parameter-tuning work had considered choices such as resolution, gain, and clustering, while leaving the filter itself without an optimization method. The authors build on a framework that incorporates topology into optimization and introduce a relaxed, more general version of Mapper to make their proposed scheme possible.

They investigate the convergence properties of this generalized representation and demonstrate filter optimization on several datasets. The resulting representations outperform arbitrary choices in the reported demonstrations. The contribution is therefore a way to make a central modeling decision responsive to an optimization objective, reducing reliance on manually choosing the function that shapes the visualization.
icml-2024-differentiable-mapper-for-topo.tldr: A relaxed Mapper construction enables optimization of the filter function that determines a dataset’s topological graph representation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether offline reinforcement learning can recover several distinct ways to solve one task. Its starting point is evidence from online reinforcement learning that learning multiple behaviors can be useful, including for adapting to a new environment with few examples. The authors identify the corresponding offline problem as insufficiently explored by existing methods.

They propose algorithms aimed specifically at learning multiple solutions from a single task and investigate their behavior experimentally. The objective makes diversity among solutions a central part of the learning problem. Success therefore involves obtaining meaningfully different behaviors, rather than treating several learned outputs as interchangeable instances of the same solution.

The experiments show solutions that differ both qualitatively and quantitatively. That finding supports the feasibility of discovering behavioral variety in the offline setting examined. The motivation includes potential adaptation benefits suggested by online learning, but the stated empirical result concerns discovery of distinct solutions itself. The paper thus establishes a basis for studying how a collection of solutions can be learned within offline reinforcement learning.
icml-2024-discovering-multiple-solutions.tldr: The proposed offline reinforcement-learning algorithms discover multiple qualitatively and quantitatively distinct solutions to a single task.

paragraphs: DITTO controls a pretrained text-to-music diffusion model by optimizing the initial noise from which generation begins. This moves control into inference time: the underlying model does not need fine-tuning for the demonstrated tasks. The target is expressed through a differentiable feature-matching loss, allowing optimization to steer the generated music toward desired properties.

The framework supports a wide range of musical edits and constraints. Demonstrations include filling missing passages, extending existing audio, creating loops, and controlling intensity, melody, or musical structure. These applications share the same basic mechanism of adjusting the starting latent noise according to a target loss. Gradient checkpointing helps make that optimization more memory efficient.

The authors compare DITTO with methods based on training, guidance, and optimization. They report state-of-the-art performance on nearly all evaluated tasks, including advantages over comparable approaches in controllability, audio quality, and computational efficiency. The findings suggest that optimizing a model’s starting point can provide flexible musical control while preserving the practical benefit of reusing an already trained generator.
icml-2024-ditto-diffusion-inference-time.tldr: DITTO steers pretrained music diffusion models by optimizing their initial noise, enabling varied editing and control tasks without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether language models resemble human learners in how they make mistakes on arithmetic word problems. The question matters for using these models to study cognition: producing plausible answers does not by itself establish that a model shares the biases of people. The authors focus specifically on biases documented in children.

Drawing on learning-science literature, they divide problem solving into three stages: understanding the text, planning a solution, and carrying out the arithmetic. They create separate tests for each stage using newly generated word problems. A neuro-symbolic generation approach provides fine-grained control over problem features, helping the tests distinguish different parts of the solving process.

The results provide evidence of human-like biases in text comprehension and solution planning for models both with and without instruction-tuning. The same resemblance does not appear in the final arithmetic-execution stage. This makes the conclusion selective: the tested models reflect some documented aspects of children’s problem solving, while their behavior differs at another stage of the same task.
icml-2024-do-language-models-exhibit-the.tldr: Language models show evidence of children’s biases in understanding and planning arithmetic word problems, but not in executing the arithmetic.

paragraphs: Classification models are commonly trained by minimizing cross-entropy, but this paper explores a broader family of objectives based on f-divergences. The authors take a Bayesian perspective, expressing classification as a maximum a posteriori probability problem. This provides the starting point for deriving alternative objectives rather than treating cross-entropy as the default formulation.

They use a variational representation of f-divergence to construct a class of training objectives. They also take a bottom-up approach to developing an additional objective associated with a new divergence called shifted log, or SL. The contribution therefore includes both a general formulation and a particular member designed to improve classification performance.

The paper analyzes the proposed objectives theoretically and evaluates them on toy examples, image datasets, and signal detection or decoding problems. Across these settings, the results support the approach, with SL achieving the highest classification accuracy in almost all considered cases. This is evidence that the choice of divergence can materially affect classification outcomes within the tested applications.
icml-2024-f-divergence-based-classificat.tldr: The paper derives classification objectives from f-divergences and introduces shifted log divergence, which achieves the highest accuracy in almost all evaluated cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn neural signed distance functions for three-dimensional shapes when only sparse point clouds are available and ground-truth supervision is absent. Neural signed distance functions can encode intricate geometry, but sparse observations make learning such a representation difficult. The work focuses on improving the guidance supplied during that learning process.

Existing approaches described in the abstract use smoothness priors as regularization. The proposed method introduces a regularization term built from adversarial samples around the shape. These spatial samples give the learning objective an additional way to constrain the resulting representation. The methodological contribution is this use of adversarial samples to improve the learned signed distance function.

Experiments on both synthetic and real data show improvements over baselines and state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the usefulness of the proposed regularizer under the sparse, unsupervised conditions studied. More broadly, the paper shows that how learning is constrained around a shape can be consequential when the observed points alone provide limited information about its geometry.
icml-2024-few-shot-unsupervised-implicit.tldr: Adversarial samples around a shape provide regularization that improves neural signed distance learning from sparse, unsupervised point clouds.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations store a signal in the weights of a neural network. Although this approach has applications in compression, view synthesis, and volumetric understanding, processing the resulting representations remains challenging. The paper focuses on a conceptual issue: an individual representation often stands alone, leaving the meaning of its surrounding neighborhood unclear.

The authors reformulate the model using operator theory, calling the result Operator INR, or O-INR. Instead of mapping positional encodings directly to signal values, the model maps between function spaces. Integral transforms provide a practical realization of this viewpoint. Within that construction, convolutions are sufficient, removing the need for the multilayer perceptrons used in most existing INR models.

The authors report numerical stability benefits and show that O-INR handles most problem settings considered in the literature with performance similar to baseline methods. The stated benefit is therefore a broader formulation and useful computational behavior with little, if any, performance compromise. It offers a different foundation for working with implicit representations while retaining their demonstrated practical capabilities.
icml-2024-implicit-representations-via-o.tldr: Operator INR reformulates implicit signal representations as mappings between function spaces, enabling convolution-based models with stability benefits and comparable performance.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a parameter-efficiency problem in deep reinforcement learning: agents can struggle to make effective use of the networks they already have. The authors investigate whether sparse training techniques can improve that use of capacity. Their focus is value-based agents, so the central question concerns the networks supporting value-based learning.

The proposed approach uses gradual magnitude pruning to make those networks sparse. This brings a parameter-reduction technique into the effort to improve learning performance itself. The paper frames pruning as a way to maximize parameter effectiveness, connecting earlier insights about sparse training with the particular difficulty of using neural-network capacity in reinforcement learning.

The reported result is a substantial performance improvement over traditional networks while retaining only a small fraction of the full parameter count. These findings make model size and agent performance separate considerations in the studied setting: keeping more parameters did not deliver the stronger result. The contribution is empirical evidence that gradual magnitude pruning can improve both parameter economy and the performance of value-based agents.
icml-2024-in-value-based-deep-reinforcem.tldr: Gradual magnitude pruning substantially improves the reported performance of value-based reinforcement-learning agents while retaining only a small fraction of their parameters.

paragraphs: Many neuron-interpretation methods explain a neuron by examining inputs that produce its strongest activations. This paper argues that such examples provide an incomplete account. The authors find that the highest activation range contributes only a small share of the neuron’s causal effect, making it an insufficient basis for understanding the neuron’s overall role.

They also show that inputs producing lower activations can be very different from the strongest examples. Those responses cannot reliably be predicted just by inspecting high activations. To capture a broader range of behavior, the paper proposes describing a neuron as a linear combination of concepts and introduces an efficient method for generating such explanations.

The authors additionally develop an automatic evaluation approach in vision: use the explanation to predict a neuron’s activations on previously unseen inputs. This treats explanation quality as something that can be checked through simulation. The contribution connects a richer description of neuronal behavior with a test of whether that description actually predicts responses beyond the examples used to form it.
icml-2024-linear-explanations-for-indivi.tldr: Describing neurons as linear combinations of concepts captures behavior missed by explanations based only on their strongest activations.

paragraphs: L-MAC aims to make an audio classifier’s decisions understandable through explanations that people can listen to. Audio poses a communication challenge for interpretability: identifying relevant evidence is useful only if that evidence can also be conveyed meaningfully. The method adds a decoder on top of a pretrained classifier to produce binary masks selecting relevant portions of the input.

The decoder learns through a two-sided objective. The selected audio should preserve strong confidence in the classifier’s decision, while the excluded audio should reduce the probability of that output. This tests both what the explanation retains and what it leaves behind, tying the mask to the behavior of the classifier being explained.

Quantitative evaluations on data both within and outside the original domain show more faithful interpretations than several gradient-based and masking-based methods. A user study also finds that participants prefer L-MAC’s explanations on average. These results address complementary goals: representing the classifier’s decision faithfully and producing an explanation whose audible form users find preferable.
icml-2024-listenable-maps-for-audio-clas.tldr: L-MAC learns audio masks that produce listenable explanations with stronger measured faithfulness and higher average user preference than the compared methods.

paragraphs: MADA addresses the difficulty of choosing an optimizer that works well across different deep-learning tasks. Many alternatives to Adam perform well in some settings without consistently improving on it everywhere. The paper introduces a framework that represents several known optimizers within a parameterized space and searches that space while model training is underway.

The search uses hyper-gradient descent to adapt the optimizer itself. The authors also introduce AVGrad, a modification of AMSGrad that replaces a maximum operation with averaging, making it more suitable for this optimization process. Together, these ideas allow the training procedure to adjust how it updates model parameters as learning proceeds.

Experiments on vision and language tasks show MADA outperforming Adam and other compared optimizers, including with imperfectly tuned hyperparameters. GPT-2 training and fine-tuning show larger validation improvements over Adam than the other optimizers deliver. A convergence analysis further shows that parameterized interpolations can improve error bounds up to constants, offering theoretical support for the potential benefit of adapting among optimizers.
icml-2024-mada-meta-adaptive-optimizers-.tldr: MADA uses hyper-gradient descent to adapt the optimizer during training and reports improvements across the evaluated vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: Increasing model size has been a productive strategy in supervised and self-supervised learning, where empirical scaling relationships help describe improvements. Reinforcement learning has been less predictable: adding parameters can even reduce final performance. This paper investigates whether changing the architecture of value-based networks can make larger parameter counts more useful.

The authors incorporate mixture-of-experts modules, emphasizing Soft MoEs, into those networks. The experiment concerns the organization of model capacity as well as its amount. By testing this architectural change across different model sizes and training regimes, they examine whether additional parameters can translate into more reliable performance gains in the studied reinforcement-learning settings.

The results show substantial performance increases and models that scale more effectively with parameter count. The authors present this as strong empirical evidence toward developing scaling laws for reinforcement learning. That conclusion concerns progress toward such laws: the reported contribution is an architectural route to improved scaling behavior across the tested conditions, rather than a universal relationship already established for reinforcement learning.
icml-2024-mixtures-of-experts-unlock-par.tldr: Adding mixture-of-experts modules to value-based networks makes increased parameter counts more beneficial across the tested reinforcement-learning settings.

paragraphs: This paper examines how class labels can improve asymmetric non-contrastive learning, or ANCL, a family of methods for learning representations of data. The motivation is a gap between learning settings: ANCL often outperforms contrastive approaches in self-supervised learning, but its use with explicit supervision has received less attention.

The authors introduce supervised ANCL methods called SupSiam and SupBYOL. These methods incorporate labels into representation learning. The proposed framework improves the learned representations while avoiding collapse, the failure in which representations lose the distinctions that make them useful. This makes retaining useful differences an important part of the reported result.

Their analysis finds that supervision reduces variation among representations belonging to the same class. In plain language, examples sharing a label become more alike in the learned representation. However, the authors also find that the contribution of supervision should be adjusted to obtain the best performance; the finding does not imply that stronger supervision is always better.

Experiments report advantages for supervised ANCL across multiple datasets and tasks. These findings support incorporating labels into ANCL, with the balance of supervision playing a role in how effectively the resulting representations perform.
icml-2024-on-the-effectiveness-of-superv.tldr: SupSiam and SupBYOL incorporate labels into asymmetric non-contrastive learning, improving representations without collapse while showing that the contribution of supervision should be adjusted.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization-based account of how spiking neurons evolve in discrete time. Spiking neural networks are studied for energy-efficient inference and for simulating neural mechanisms, but limited discrete theory constrains their practical performance and support for nonlinear functions. The authors address that gap by relating neuron dynamics to familiar optimization procedures.

They prove that the discrete dynamics of simple integrate-and-fire models approximate the subgradient method for unconstrained optimization problems. Building on that result, they introduce neuronal dynamics based on sign gradient descent. The new formulation can approximate a range of nonlinearities beyond ReLU and improves conversion from conventional neural networks to spiking networks using few time steps.

Experiments on large-scale datasets report state-of-the-art conversion performance. The authors also report the first conversions of architectures including ConvNext, MLP-Mixer, and ResMLP. These findings connect the theoretical interpretation to practical architectural coverage: a broader model of neuronal dynamics supports conversion of networks whose nonlinear behavior extends beyond the previously emphasized ReLU setting.
icml-2024-sign-gradient-descent-based-ne.tldr: An optimization-based model of spiking dynamics enables broader nonlinearities and improves low-time-step conversion from conventional to spiking neural networks.

paragraphs: SILVER targets a computational bottleneck in variance-reduced optimization: repeatedly calculating full gradients can be expensive, especially in distributed systems. The paper introduces a single-loop gradient estimator for finite-sum, non-convex problems. It avoids repeated full-gradient calculations while still achieving the stated optimal gradient complexity.

The theoretical results go beyond a basic convergence guarantee. SILVER provably reaches second-order optimality, achieves exponential convergence within a Polyak–Łojasiewicz region, and can gain additional speed depending on data heterogeneity. The regional condition matters: the exponential convergence claim applies where that mathematical property holds. The heterogeneity-dependent result also makes the relationship among data sources relevant to computational performance.

The authors then combine SILVER with local updates to design federated-learning algorithms that reduce communication. They report the best communication-round and communicated-gradient bounds across the full range of Hessian heterogeneity considered, while preserving second-order optimality and exponential convergence in the PL region. This links the estimator’s optimization guarantees to the cost of coordinating learning across participants.
icml-2024-silver-single-loop-variance-re.tldr: SILVER avoids repeated full gradients while providing strong non-convex convergence guarantees and communication-efficient federated-learning methods.

paragraphs: Skill Set Optimization improves a language-model actor by turning rewarding experience into a reusable collection of skills. The problem is how to use feedback from an interactive environment for continued improvement. SSO makes that feedback actionable through instructions placed in the actor’s context, allowing successful behaviors to inform later decisions.

The method identifies recurring segments of trajectories associated with high rewards. It then generates subgoals and instructions that describe each segment as a skill. Refinement continues after construction: skills that stop producing high rewards are pruned from the collection. This gives the skill set a feedback-driven update process rather than leaving it as a fixed record of past successes.

The authors evaluate SSO in NetHack and ScienceWorld, demonstrating optimization of the skill collection and in-context policy improvement. They report a 40% improvement over baselines on their custom NetHack task and a 35% improvement over the previous state of the art in ScienceWorld. These results support the use of constructed and selectively retained skills to improve the tested language-model actors.
icml-2024-skill-set-optimization-reinfor.tldr: SSO converts rewarding behavior into reusable in-context skills and prunes ineffective skills to improve language-model actors.

paragraphs: Static sparse training starts with a network in which only selected connections are trainable. A binary mask defines this subnetwork, and many initialization methods choose that mask around an already initialized dense model. This paper argues that the weights within the sparse subnetwork also deserve direct attention because their initialization affects optimization.

The proposed Exact Orthogonal Initialization, or EOI, composes random Givens rotations to produce sparse orthogonal weights. Orthogonality is motivated by its ability to help stabilize gradient signals. The method provides exact rather than approximate orthogonality and allows layers to be created at arbitrary densities, connecting a mathematical property of the weights with control over sparsity.

Experiments show improvements in effectiveness and efficiency over common sparse initialization techniques. Particularly striking demonstrations train highly sparse, 1,000-layer multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks without residual connections or normalization. These results emphasize that successful static sparse training depends on how the retained connections are initialized as well as on which connections the mask selects.
icml-2024-sparser-better-deeper-stronger.tldr: Exact Orthogonal Initialization improves static sparse training and enables highly sparse 1,000-layer networks without residual connections or normalization.

paragraphs: This paper develops quantum algorithms for sampling distributions proportional to exp(−βf(x)) and for estimating their partition functions. The distributions may be non-logconcave, extending the target beyond that structural restriction. When f is a finite sum, the algorithms can use a stochastic gradient oracle based on mini-batches, implementing the quantum walk operations inexactly.

A central analytical difficulty is that the resulting Markov chains generally do not satisfy detailed balance. This prevents the authors from expressing mixing time through the spectral gap of the transition density matrix in the usual way. They instead construct a reversible reference chain that converges to the desired distribution and use it to bound the discrepancy between the algorithm’s output and its target.

That reference chain provides the bridge needed to establish total complexity despite the inexact operations and lack of detailed balance. Under similar assumptions, the resulting quantum algorithms offer polynomial speedups in dimension or precision dependence over the best-known classical algorithms. The advantage is therefore a conditional complexity comparison for the specified sampling and estimation problems.
icml-2024-stochastic-quantum-sampling-fo.tldr: Quantum sampling and partition-function algorithms achieve polynomial dimension or precision speedups under comparable assumptions, including for possibly non-logconcave targets.

paragraphs: StructChem addresses complex chemistry problems that require knowledge, precise calculation, and reasoning about interacting concepts. The authors find that even advanced language models can fail in multiple ways on these tasks. Their analysis points to an organizational problem: errors often arise because the model lacks an effective reasoning structure, rather than because it lacks the necessary chemistry knowledge.

The proposed prompting strategy guides the model to retrieve relevant knowledge, incorporate it into step-by-step reasoning, and iteratively refine the result. This structure is intended to help the model use what it knows in a coordinated way. The intervention therefore focuses on the process through which an answer is developed.

Tests cover quantum chemistry, mechanics, physical chemistry, and kinetics. StructChem substantially improves GPT-4’s performance, with a reported peak improvement of up to 30%. That figure describes the maximum reported gain, rather than a uniform improvement across all settings. The analysis also identifies continuing difficulties with precise, grounded scientific reasoning, showing why improved prompting is useful while further research remains necessary.
icml-2024-structured-chemistry-reasoning.tldr: StructChem structures knowledge retrieval, step-by-step reasoning, and refinement to improve language-model performance on complex chemistry problems.

paragraphs: Image-restoration methods often pursue two goals simultaneously: produce a perceptually convincing image and keep that reconstruction consistent with the available measurements. This paper studies deterministic methods and proves that improving both goals carries a robustness cost. The result applies regardless of the particular degradation involved in the imaging problem.

The proof relates those goals to the model’s Lipschitz constant, which describes how strongly its output can change when its input changes. Better joint perceptual quality and measurement consistency require a larger constant. As both approach perfection, the constant must grow without bound. The authors connect this necessary increase in sensitivity to greater susceptibility to adversarial attacks.

The paper demonstrates the theory using single-image super-resolution in both noisy and noiseless settings. It also shows that the same sensitivity can be useful: exploiting it allows exploration of the posterior distribution and lets a deterministic model imitate stochastic methods. The work thus identifies a fundamental tradeoff and a way to put its otherwise undesirable behavior to use.
icml-2024-the-perception-robustness-trad.tldr: Deterministic restoration methods must become more sensitive as perceptual quality and measurement consistency jointly approach perfection.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to reuse parameter-efficient language-model adapters for new tasks. It treats adapters as a library whose contents must be organized and whose relevant components must be selected for each input. The study covers both building that library from multitask data and generalizing through routing in zero-shot and supervised settings.

For library construction, the authors introduce model-based clustering, or MBC. It groups tasks using similarities among adapter parameters, indirectly targeting transfer across the multitask dataset. For reuse, they introduce Arrow, a zero-shot routing mechanism that dynamically selects relevant adapters for new inputs without retraining. These methods address complementary parts of making adapter collections useful.

Experiments with models including Phi-2 and Mistral span a broad collection of held-out tasks. The results show stronger generalization from MBC-based adapters and Arrow routing. The authors frame this as progress toward modular language models that can match or outperform traditional joint training, suggesting that organizing and selecting reusable components can support adaptation to tasks outside the original training collection.
icml-2024-towards-modular-llms-by-buildi.tldr: MBC organizes adapter libraries and Arrow selects adapters without retraining, improving generalization to held-out language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines the expressive power of sequence models that combine linear recurrent computations with position-wise multilayer perceptrons. Such architectures have shown strong practical performance, but their theoretical capabilities and the role of particular design choices remain less understood. The authors focus on diagonal linear recurrences, considering both real and complex-valued versions.

They prove that combining these recurrences with multilayer perceptrons permits arbitrarily accurate approximation of regular causal sequence-to-sequence maps. The proof separates two jobs: the recurrent component encodes the input sequence without losing information, and the nonlinear component processes that encoding. This explains how a linear recurrence can participate in an expressive nonlinear sequence model.

Real diagonal recurrences are sufficient for the stated universality result. However, the authors also prove that complex eigenvalues near the unit disk substantially help information storage. They connect this benefit with vanishing gradients and provide supporting experiments. The distinction matters: a design choice can improve information retention in practice even when it is not required for theoretical universality.
icml-2024-universality-of-linear-recurre.tldr: Linear diagonal recurrences followed by nonlinear projections are universal for regular causal sequence maps, while suitable complex eigenvalues improve information storage.

paragraphs: The Linearized Laplace Approximation adds predictive uncertainty estimates to pretrained neural networks, but its computational cost can grow burdensome with dataset size or parameter count. Existing shortcuts introduce additional approximations that may compromise performance. This paper proposes a variational sparse Gaussian-process approach to making the approximation more efficient.

The method uses a dual reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space formulation of Gaussian processes and preserves the original neural network’s output as the predictive mean. It also supports efficient stochastic optimization. The authors report sublinear training time with respect to dataset size and, more specifically, a training cost independent of the number of training points.

Experiments on regression and classification compare the method with accelerated LLA, which uses a Nyström approximation, and other efficient variants based on sample-then-optimize procedures. The proposed approach improves both predictive-distribution quality and total computation time in those comparisons. Its contribution is therefore a more efficient route to uncertainty estimation that retains the pretrained network’s mean prediction while improving the reported uncertainty–computation balance.
icml-2024-variational-linearized-laplace.tldr: A variational sparse Gaussian-process approximation makes Linearized Laplace uncertainty estimation faster while preserving the original network’s predictive mean.
